tagline: Rivers lead a trade road into the mountains toward Quebec.
intro: Old Canada Road follows U.S. 201 between Solon and the Canadian border, beside rivers and into forested mountains. The 78-mile paved, two-lane drive has seven interpretive rest areas and turnouts beside cliffs and water. The Federal Highway Administration lists it as a National Scenic Byway and describes a journey through mountain ridges, forests and rivers, tracing travel between Maine and Quebec. It allows 2.5 hours for the drive, or a day to enjoy the byway. Wyman Dam, built in 1930 from earth and concrete, stands 155 feet high across the Kennebec.

The corridor follows old Abenaki river trading routes. Massachusetts funded the Canada Road to connect farming districts with Quebec City for trade. In the 1830s, Maine hired Captain James Jackman to build the road connecting the United States and Canada; the town of Jackman carries his name. International commercial trucks continue to use the route heavily.

Heading north from Solon, the southern stretch follows the eastern side of the Kennebec and man-made Wyman Lake to The Forks, where the Dead River joins the Kennebec. Beyond The Forks, U.S. 201 leaves the river, climbs over Johnson Mountain and passes Coburn Mountain. Attean Pond Lookout precedes the descent into Jackman; Moose River and Dennistown follow before the border crossing.

moments.title: The Forks
moments.text: The Dead River meets the Kennebec at The Forks, a plantation with 48 residents counted in the 2020 census. Dam-controlled releases help make this a whitewater rafting destination. The river junction also marks a change in the drive: U.S. 201 leaves the Kennebec here and heads into the north woods mountains. For a closer look at the water, the graveled Dead River trail runs beside its namesake river just north of the confluence. The Appalachian Trail crosses the southern part of the plantation. The Dead River trail also has picnic tables, and part of it is wheelchair accessible.

moments.title: Attean Pond Lookout
moments.text: Attean Pond Lookout marks the high point of the road before its descent into Jackman. The climb north from The Forks has taken U.S. 201 over Johnson Mountain and past Coburn Mountain. From the overlook just south of town, the view includes Moose River Valley, Attean Pond and the border mountains. Connecting rivers and streams extend toward the Canadian border, bringing the waterways back into view after the mountain climb.
moments.notice: Moose River Valley, Attean Pond and the border mountains share the view.

moments.title: Jackman
moments.text: Jackman takes its name from a road builder: Captain James Jackman, hired by Maine in the 1830s to connect the United States with Canada. Another international connection arrived in 1889, when the International Railway of Maine linked the town to the Canadian Pacific network. A logging railroad followed in 1915, carrying timber to the Jackman sawmill until 1926. Passenger trains stopped serving Jackman in 1981, returned in 1985 and ceased service again in 1994. U.S. 201 continues north from town with State Route 6 for the remaining 16.4 miles to the border.
